faqs.q: What should I expect to pay for wildlife removal in Manhattan?
faqs.a: The price turns on the species, the number of entry points, and whether young or cleanup are involved. A single squirrel entry sealed early is a much smaller job than a raccoon family or a bat colony. We inspect, explain the full scope, and quote it in writing before work starts.

faqs.q: When do animals get into Manhattan attics most often?
faqs.a: Our crew's Manhattan work centers on Norway rats in basements and trash rooms, pigeons on ledges and signs, and raccoons at the Central Park edges. The pattern follows the housing and the habitat: central park keeps animals close, and once one finds a way into a roofline, chimney, or crawlspace here, it usually comes back until every entry is sealed. That is why we pair removal with proofing on every Manhattan job rather than just taking the animal out.

Manhattan.wildlife_intro:
Manhattan keeps our crew busy with Norway rats in basements and trash rooms, pigeons on ledges and signs, and raccoons at the Central Park edges. Central Park  gives wildlife food, water, and cover within a short run of almost every roof in town, and the housing does the rest — once an animal finds a soft soffit, an uncapped chimney, or a gap at the roofline, it treats the house as part of its territory.

The year has a rhythm in Manhattan. Fall pushes squirrels, raccoons, and rodents indoors ahead of winter; spring brings denning mothers looking for chimneys and attic corners; summer is when bat colonies are most visible in older homes and when young animals start ranging on their own. Most Manhattan jobs start with a full roofline and foundation inspection, then removal and sealing every entry we find, because closing only the obvious hole rarely holds.
